overview: This file documents the Freeport Sulphur Company’s July 1947 request to send technical representatives to occupied Japan to investigate sulphur deposits and potentially acquire operating rights. Company president Langbourne M. Williams, Jr. argued that Japanese production could alleviate a worldwide sulphur shortage, create employment, meet domestic requirements, and earn foreign exchange through exports. State Department correspondence and an internal memorandum show officials consulting the War Department, distinguishing the proposed mission from the newly authorized entry of ordinary traders, and considering a special permit from the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP). Although officials regarded expanded sulphur production favorably, they warned that economic instability had led the State Department to support a temporary moratorium on foreign investment in Japan.

subfiles.title: Freeport application to investigate Japanese sulphur deposits
subfiles.from: Langbourne M. Williams, Jr., President, Freeport Sulphur Company
subfiles.to: Robert A. Lovett, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Williams requests permission to send a small technical party to investigate Japanese sulphur deposits and assess the possibility of obtaining operating rights.
subfiles.summary: Williams describes sulphur as an essential input for fertilizer, steel, paper, rayon, rubber, petroleum refining, pesticides, and explosives, and reports that worldwide demand exceeds Freeport’s available supply. He notes that Japan produced about 200,000 tons annually before the war and argues that American development of its deposits could supply Japanese needs, support exports, earn foreign exchange, and create employment. Freeport proposes sending two mining engineers and probably one additional representative to study reserves, ore grades, operating conditions, and costs before seeking rights to promising properties.

subfiles.title: Draft Lovett reply concerning the Freeport application
subfiles.about: Lovett advises Williams that the Department has prepared guidance and offers to arrange a Washington meeting if Freeport sends a representative.
subfiles.summary: Lovett states that he referred Williams’s July 8 letter to the appropriate State Department division. He encloses a memorandum describing the preferred course of action and offers to arrange a meeting in Washington if Williams provides advance notice that a company representative will attend.

subfiles.title: Final Lovett reply inviting consultation in Washington
subfiles.from: Robert A. Lovett, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The final version of Lovett’s reply transmits departmental guidance and offers to arrange an official meeting in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Addressing Williams personally as “Lang,” Lovett repeats that the July 8 request was referred to the appropriate division. He encloses a memorandum on the recommended procedure and offers to arrange a meeting if Freeport chooses to send a representative to Washington. Drafting and clearance notations dated July 17 and July 25 accompany the copy, while July 28 appears as the prominent final date stamp.

subfiles.title: Martin memorandum on entry permits and foreign investment
subfiles.about: Martin assesses Freeport’s proposal, recommends interdepartmental discussions, and identifies restrictions on entry and foreign investment in occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: Martin reports that the State Department consulted the War Department and concluded that Freeport’s proposed technical mission did not fall within the ordinary trader-entry program scheduled to begin August 15. Although the Department of Commerce was unlikely to approve the application through that program, Martin considered increased Japanese sulphur production and exports worthy of examination. He recommends inviting a company representative to confer with State and War Department officials, after which they could decide whether to seek a special SCAP entry permit. He cautions that any contemplated purchase of Japanese sulphur properties would encounter the State Department’s temporary moratorium on foreign investment because of Japan’s unstable economic conditions.

interest: The file offers a compact case study of how an American corporation attempted to enter the Japanese resource sector during the early occupation. It is especially useful for showing the bureaucratic distinction between ordinary commercial traders and technical representatives seeking access for a specific industrial project, as well as the respective roles of the State Department, War Department, Department of Commerce, and SCAP. The juxtaposition of enthusiasm for export-led reconstruction with a moratorium on foreign investment exposes a central tension in occupation economic policy: officials wanted American expertise and expanded production but remained wary of foreign acquisition of Japanese assets during a period of severe instability.
